endorsements.title: Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework: Generative AI Profile (NIST AI 600-1)
endorsements.issuer: National Institute of Standards and Technology
endorsements.quote: Define acceptable use policies for GAI interfaces, modalities, and human-AI configurations (i.e., for chatbots and decision-making tasks), including criteria for the kinds of queries GAI applications should refuse to respond to.

endorsements.title: CHAI Responsible AI Guide (Assurance Standards Guide)
endorsements.quote: It's important to note that the Safeguard LLM is programmed to reject any prompts requesting medical recommendations, such as differential diagnoses or treatment and management plans, as these requests fall outside the system's intended scope.

endorsements.title: Chatbots in medicine: certification process and applied use case
endorsements.quote: One way to mitigate these risks is by restricting chatbots to a specific knowledge base through retrieval-augmented generation (RAG).

endorsements.title: Building a Safe and Transparent Workflow for Large Language Model (LLM)-Assisted Clinical Trials and Prediction Models: A Technical Report
endorsements.quote: Define which tasks are appropriate for LLM assistance (e.g., outlining, language refinement, and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG)-based summarization) and which are excluded; record this in a governance note and in Table 2 .

endorsements.title: Fluency without understanding: risks of large language models in mental healthcare
endorsements.quote: Responsible integration therefore requires strict governance, clear task boundaries, human verification of outputs, strong privacy protections and explicit accountability when errors occur.

endorsements.title: Should I and Can I Use AI for Forensic Psychiatry Report Writing?
endorsements.quote: A forensic psychiatrist should not use AI to generate or materially shape the substantive analysis or final opinion that the court is asked to trust as expert evidence.

endorsements.title: NeonatAIlogy: The GIRISH (Goal, Input, Role, Iterative Refinement, Safety Verification, and Human Accountability) Framework for Structured, Human-Accountable Artificial Intelligence in Neonatal Intensive Care
endorsements.quote: Explicitly limiting the role reduces hallucination risk.

evidence.title: Blueprint for Safety: Implementing a Clinically Governed AI Digital Assistant for Patient Guidance
evidence.venue: NEJM catalyst innovations in care delivery
evidence.outcome: AI-generated diagnoses under guardrails restricting assistant to generalized guidance
evidence.quote: Using a randomized rollout to half of the patient population, the authors found that the risk-stratified assistant maintained a high level of clinical safety (96% accurate guidance, 0% critical safety events, and no AI-generated diagnoses) while reducing standard-risk queries routed to human support by 65%, shortening average human response times from 9.6 to 3.6 minutes, and improving resolution of health inquiries without additional visits.

evidence.title: End-to-End Clinical Validation of a Human-Supervised Large Language Model Agent for Enterprise Surgical Pathology Reporting
evidence.venue: Modern pathology : an official journal of the United States and Canadian Academy of Pathology, Inc
evidence.outcome: Diagnostic safety of LLM agent restricted to structuring and formatting, with diagnostic inference prohibited
evidence.effect: No hallucinated diagnoses identified; 2 of 94 cases (2%) showed minor diagnostic misinterpretation from descriptive container-label terms; 8 cases (8.5%) had minor formatting deviations.
evidence.quote: Two cases (2%) showed minor diagnostic misinterpretation, in which descriptive container-label terms (eg, "ulcer" and "erosion") were incorporated into diagnostic text; no hallucinated diagnoses were identified.

evidence.title: A Neuro-Symbolic Knowledge Graph and Large Language Model Hybrid Architecture for Multi-Modality Mental Health Counseling
evidence.outcome: Unsolicited clinical monologues, diagnoses and medication advice with vs without KG governance
evidence.effect: Ungoverned model produced unsolicited clinical monologues on 100% of turns vs 9% governed; delivered diagnoses and medication advice the governed system never produced.
evidence.quote: Stripped of governance, the same model produced unsolicited clinical monologues on 100% of turns (vs 9% governed) and delivered diagnoses and medication advice the governed system never produced.

evidence.title: Checkup2Action: A Multimodal Clinical Check-up Report Dataset for Patient-Oriented Action Card Generation
evidence.outcome: Problem recall and diagnostic overstatement with versus without safety constraints
evidence.effect: Removing safety constraints raised problem recall from 0.527 to 0.825 but produced more diagnostic overstatement, so the constraints trade coverage for safer patient communication.
evidence.quote: Removing safety constraints increased problem recall from 0.527 to 0.825, but produced more diagnostic overstatement.

evidence.title: Toward Trustworthy Large Language Model Agents in Healthcare
evidence.outcome: Safety compliance of scheduling agent with scope constraints refusing medical advice or diagnosis
evidence.effect: 96.0% safety compliance on the dedicated safety-critical evaluation subset; 91.8% task completion
evidence.quote: Experimental results demonstrate a 91.8% task completion rate with a median per-request latency of 2.2 seconds, 96.0% safety compliance on the dedicated safety-critical evaluation subset, and an average operational cost of $0.0324 per appointment, yielding a significant cost reduction compared to manual human scheduling.

evidence.title: TSWAP: A Multilingual Retrieval-Augmented Thai Wellness Advisor
evidence.outcome: Out-of-scope and drug-dosing responses with vs without safety prompt
evidence.effect: Without the safety prompt, the backend model family produced a full drug-dosing schedule and complied with out-of-scope requests (71-question no-retrieval probe).
evidence.quote: We release the first Thai traditional-medicine/wellness retrieval benchmark (50 questions with gold document IDs; Recall@5 = 0.88), production QA logs (91.1% test-retest pass over 259 cases), and a 71-question frontier no-retrieval probe showing what each grounding pillar contributes: without the safety prompt the backend model family produced a full drug-dosing schedule and complied with out-of-scope requests, and without the knowledge base it produced zero verifiable provider recommendations.

evidence.title: Real-world use and evaluation of a generative AI chatbot for Parkinson's disease information: a prospective observational study
evidence.outcome: Medication recommendations despite prompt prohibiting treatment advice
evidence.effect: Sampled critical events included inappropriate memantine recommendation, non-first-line amantadine recommendation, levodopa duration error, and medication misidentification
evidence.quote: All four sampled events mapped to the knowledge boundary class: an inappropriate drug recommendation for Parkinson's disease dementia (memantine), a pharmacologically inaccurate statement of prolonged-release levodopa duration, a recommendation of a non-first-line medication for tremor (amantadine), and a medication misidentification in which a levodopa/carbidopa preparation was labelled as selegiline.

evidence.title: Assessing the Limitations of Large Language Models in Clinical Practice Guideline-concordant Treatment Decision-making on Real-world Data
evidence.quote: When presented with original medical reports, LLMs showed poor performance (kappa: −0.47–0.22, ICC: 0.0–1.0, FBI: 0.95–1.51).

evidence.title: Identifying Deprescribing Opportunities With Large Language Models in Older Adults: Retrospective Cohort Study
evidence.outcome: LLM making deprescribing recommendations, including potentially harmful ones, on clinical cases
evidence.effect: Deprescribing step PPV 0.47; LLM recommended deprescribing far more often (11.6%) than students (1.91%); harmful cases observed, e.g., suggesting deprescribing anticoagulation after recent thromboembolism.
evidence.quote: Cases with the potential for human harm were observed, such as suggesting deprescribing anticoagulation in a patient with recent thromboembolism.

evidence.title: Training ChatGPT for surgical decisions: Bariatric surgery analysis using algorithms and evidence
evidence.outcome: Reliability of LLM treatment recommendations for surgical decision-making
evidence.effect: ChatGPT's surgical technique recommendations agreed poorly with clinicians (20.0% and 25.8% concordance), so it was judged not reliable for autonomous surgical decision-making.
evidence.quote: While potentially useful as an educational tool, ChatGPT is not yet reliable for autonomous surgical decision-making.

evidence.title: The impact of prompting on ChatGPT's adherence to status epilepticus treatment guidelines
evidence.effect: Guideline gaps included side positioning 25% and neurological assessments 0-25%, with false statements; authors concluded not ready for safe autonomous practice.
evidence.quote: While the model shows promise in some areas and excels with the newer LLMs, the need for explicit, structured prompts, the occasional propagation of false statements, and gaps in guideline adherence indicate that such AI systems are not yet ready to be used safely and autonomously in clinical practice.

evidence.title: Assessing the Limitations of Large Language Models in Clinical Practice Guideline-Concordant Treatment Decision-Making on Real-World Data: Retrospective Study
evidence.outcome: LLM treatment recommendation quality on real-world data
evidence.effect: LLMs gave poor agreement with the heart team on original reports and are deemed unsuitable as decision makers; some recommended heart transplantation, ignoring instructions.
evidence.quote: Overall, we conclude that LLMs are currently not suitable as decision makers for the treatment of patients with severe AS, as our results suggest that LLMs require elaborate preprocessing of patient data to make guideline-concordant treatment decisions.

evidence.title: Low-energy small language models with retrieval-augmented generation can surpass large-model performance in rheumatology
evidence.outcome: LLMs generating treatment recommendations with unsafe content
evidence.effect: 9% of responses were unsuitable for clinical use, partly from unsafe or hallucinated therapeutic recommendations; authors state no model should be used without expert supervision.
evidence.quote: As a result, none of the evaluated models should be used without expert supervision.

evidence.title: Testing Knowledge Boundaries: Adversarial Evaluation of LLMs for Antimicrobial Stewardship
evidence.venue: Clinical microbiology and infection : the official publication of the European Society of Clinical Microbiology and Infectious Diseases
evidence.effect: Danger flags ranged from 6.7% to 16.7% across models.
evidence.quote: Danger flags ranged from 6.7% to 16.7% across models, with no significant difference between commercial and open-weight models.

evidence.title: Trivial Prompt Reframing Bypasses Safety Guardrails in Googleś MedGemma-4B
evidence.outcome: Model providing dosages, diagnoses, treatments, and drug interaction judgments despite prohibited behaviors
evidence.effect: Overall ASR 38.0% across guarded concepts; drug-interaction guardrail nearly absent at 83.2% ASR.
evidence.quote: Under the primary LLM judge the overall Attack Success Rate (ASR, the fraction coded comply) is 38.0%.

evidence.title: Deterministic Retrieval-Grounded Language Models for Clinical Counseling: Large-Scale Multilingual Evaluation with Cryptographically Verifiable Pipelines
evidence.effect: No unintended diagnostic outputs were observed across 1,895 English and Chinese scenarios.
evidence.quote: No system failures or unintended diagnostic outputs were observed across either evaluation.

commentary.bottom_line: Six studies test scope restriction with refusal criteria, and five of them, including one randomized trial in real deployment, report few or no diagnostic and treatment outputs under the constraint. Hazard studies in which prohibitions were already in place suggest that restriction may reduce out-of-scope advice without eliminating it.

perspectives.view: One randomized trial in real deployment reported no AI-generated diagnoses and 96% accurate guidance, but it did not report sample size or population. A prospective study of 94 biopsy cases found no hallucinated diagnoses and 2% minor misinterpretation. The other four tests are simulations or benchmarks. Indirectness and imprecision support a low certainty rating.

A governed model gave unsolicited clinical monologues on 9% of turns, compared with 100% for an ungoverned model. In 2,035 German conversations, a prompt prohibiting treatment advice still yielded medication errors. A benchmark found a 38.0% attack success rate against prohibited behaviors. Prompt-only refusal criteria may leak, so deployers may need output monitoring as well.

In a real pathology workflow, an agent restricted to formatting produced minor formatting deviations in 8.5% of cases. A scheduling agent with scope constraints reached 96.0% safety compliance and 91.8% task completion, but only in 680 simulated benchmark scenarios. Live workflow evidence comes from the pathology study and the randomized trial alone.

Removing safety constraints raised problem recall from 0.527 to 0.825 across 2,000 check-up reports and also increased diagnostic overstatement. Tighter refusal criteria may therefore cause the assistant to surface fewer findings. Health systems may need to plan for clinician review of what the tool declines or omits.

In a 165-question Thai benchmark, the model without a safety prompt produced a full drug-dosing schedule. In a real deployment of 2,035 German conversations with non-English speakers and older adults, a prompt prohibiting treatment advice still produced medication recommendations. No test of the practice enrolled Medicaid, safety-net, or low-literacy populations.

NIST AI 600-1 asks deployers to define criteria for queries that generative AI should refuse. The CHAI guide describes a model programmed to reject diagnosis and treatment requests. These are framework statements. None of the supplied studies tests whether written acceptable-use policies change how deployed systems behave.

Hazard studies report harmful outputs, such as advice to stop anticoagulation after a recent thromboembolism and heart transplantation recommendations given despite instructions. No study of the practice measured whether refused users were directed to a clinician. The effect of refusals on patients' access to human care is unknown.

commentary.research_gap: No study measured whether refusals route patients or clinicians to a human. None tested whether refusals hold against adversarial or ambiguous requests in live deployment. Trials in Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, and low-literacy settings, with reported sample sizes and harm outcomes, would address the main gaps.
commentary.underserved_note: Among tests of the practice, only an offline benchmark of 165 questions in Thailand included non-English users, and the randomized trial did not report its population. A real-deployment hazard study in Germany with non-English speakers found that a prompt prohibition did not prevent medication recommendations. No test included Medicaid, safety-net, or low-literacy populations, so the findings may not transfer to those patients.
